claims.text: The ball-milled Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co powder is a metastable BCC solid solution.
The initial BCC powder has high lattice strain.
The initial powder has a nanocrystalline grain size below 50 nm.
Significant oxygen is trapped at grain boundaries in the ball-milled powder.
Sintering at 900–980 °C triggers transient, non-equilibrium precipitation of an (Al,Ti)-rich B2-type phase.
The B2 precipitates form a continuous, percolating nanocrystalline network.
The B2 network forms preferentially at original powder-particle boundaries and triple junctions.
Enhanced diffusion activity at 900–980 °C causes Al and Ti to segregate to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation of Al and Ti nucleates the B2 phase.
The B2 phase has significantly lower diffusion coefficients for Mg and O than the BCC matrix.
The B2 network physically blocks Mg evaporation pathways.
The B2 network retards inward oxygen diffusion.
The diffusion barrier changes oxidation from a reaction-controlled, spalling-MgO regime to a diffusion-controlled regime with a stable Al2O3/TiO2-rich scale.
The proposed sintering window produces bulk material with greater than 98% theoretical density.
The proposed sintering window increases Vickers hardness by more than 30% relative to material sintered below 800 °C.
The parabolic oxidation rate constant is one order of magnitude lower than for samples sintered at 800 °C or 1000 °C.
Samples sintered below 800 °C remain porous and have low hardness because diffusion is insufficient for densification and phase separation.
Sintering at 1000 °C causes severe Mg loss, compositional inhomogeneity, porosity, loss of the Al/Ti-rich barrier, and poor oxidation resistance.
The proposed mechanism fails above 990 °C or for holding times exceeding 20 minutes because Mg volatilization overcomes the precipitate barrier.
Exceeding the temperature or time boundary dissolves the B2 network and produces a porous, Mg-depleted matrix.
